Title: A First Look at the Security Issues in the Model Context Protocol Ecosystem
Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as a standard for connecting large language models (LLMs) with external tools. However, this MCP ecosystem introduces new security risks across hosts, servers, and registries. In this paper, we present the first cross-entity security study of MCP under a two-stage attack surface. At the registry-level, weak vetting and ownership checks allow adversarial or hijacked servers to enter hosts. After integration, attacker-controlled tool metadata can shape LLM reasoning and induce attacker-intended operations, which hosts execute without independent verification. Code-level vulnerabilities (e.g., code injection) are not required but can amplify attacker-controlled parameters into exploitation. We analyze 67,057 servers across six public registries and identify widespread conditions enabling server hijacking and invocation manipulation. We further implement MCPInspect, a pre-integration analysis tool that detects misleading tool metadata and exploitable code vulnerabilities, identifying 833 vulnerable servers and 18 with suspicious descriptions.
Major_Contribution_Result: The paper presents a cross-entity security study of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) across hosts, servers, and registries under a two-stage attack surface: weak registry vetting/ownership enabling adversarial or hijacked servers, then attacker-controlled tool metadata shaping LLM reasoning into host-executed operations without independent verification. The authors analyze 67,057 servers across six public registries and report widespread conditions enabling server hijacking and invocation manipulation. They implement MCPInspect for pre-integration analysis and report identifying 833 vulnerable servers and 18 with suspicious descriptions. Qualitative host analysis includes unexpected tool-confusion behavior (e.g., Cursor invoking the first-listed tool despite LLM selection).
Research_Limitations_Challenges: In Limitations and Future Work, the authors state that tool extraction currently focuses on tools added through explicit specifications (e.g., @server.list_tools()) and cannot yet correctly extract tools added dynamically from lists (e.g., in loops). The vulnerability summary generator uses default Semgrep rules for MCP servers, which may lead to false positives. They plan future work to trace dynamic tool lists and to build MCP-specific detection rules.
Critics: This is an ecosystem measurement and tooling paper for MCP supply-chain and host invocation integrity, not a controlled end-to-end agent-defense benchmark with standardized ASR against a fixed attack suite. The empirical claims center on registry/server census counts and illustrative host behaviors; readers should not treat those as universal agent ASR metrics. It covers a critical pre-execution trust slice for agent tool ecosystems, but does not itself provide a gate-complete mitigation–reassessment loop for deployed LLM agents.
